schools.summary: Clarke lays out the whole arc of the reign in advance — the good beginning, the Edomite war, the hired Israelites dismissed, the turn to idolatry, the disastrous challenge to Joash, and death at Lachish.
Henry reads the reign as the tragedy of half-heartedness: Amaziah did right but not with a perfect heart, a cool and indifferent friend to religion in a Laodicean age.

themes: the arc of the whole reign
right but not with a perfect heart

schools.summary: Clarke marks the descent from a fair beginning to idolatry; Wesley diagnoses a cool and indifferent friend of religion whose heart was not whole with God.
Keil and Delitzsch read 'right, but not with a perfect heart' as the interpretive key to a reign whose shallow religion will not hold under pride and victory.
Henry's Laodicean verdict: he did good but not with the heart, no enemy to religion but a friend without zeal.

themes: right but not with a perfect heart
a good beginning, a bad end

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'the sovereignty was confirmed to him'; Keil fixes the slain as the courtiers who had murdered Joash in the previous reign, executed once the throne was secure.
Henry defends the execution as necessary justice, yet insists the murderers, though perhaps avenging the prophet Zechariah, were no lawful avengers and took God's work out of his hands.
Clarke pairs the execution with the sparing of the children in v.4 as a single, deliberately limited act of justice.
Keil and Ellicott ground the sparing of the children in Deuteronomy 24:16 and the parallel at 2 Kings 14:6, Ellicott noting the chronicler's plural where Kings has the singular.
Henry praises the king for forbidding the death of the children for their parents' sin.
Clarke marks the sparing of the children as the counterpart to the execution of the murderers.

themes: mercy that contrasts with later cruelty

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott detail the census of 300,000 from twenty years up (cf. Numbers 1:2), a total far below Jehoshaphat's and half of Asa's, plausibly reduced by the wars of Joram, Ahaziah, and Joash.
Clarke: the king mustered his strength before opening the Edomite war.
Gill notes the gathering of Judah for the coming campaign.
Henry reads the shrunken muster — a quarter of Jehoshaphat's — as the weakening cost of national sin.

Keil sets the hiring as the occasion of the prophet's warning; Ellicott reckons the hundred talents near forty thousand pounds, notes the suspect number, and cites Thenius that the hiring is historical though absent from Kings.
Gill: judging his own army insufficient for Edom, Amaziah bought a hundred thousand men of the ten tribes.
Henry: had he consulted a prophet or history he would not have hired them — rashness makes work for repentance.
Ellicott glosses 'to wit, all the children of Ephraim' as defining Israel by the prophets' name for the north (Hosea 5:11), and sets the rebuke beside 2 Chronicles 19:2 and 16:7.
Clarke cites the Targum that the Word of the LORD is not the helper of Ephraim; Wesley: dangerous to associate with those from whom the Lord is departed.
Gill records and dismisses the rabbinic guess that the unnamed man of God was Amos, Isaiah's father.
Henry: no good can be expected from allies who have not God with them nor his blessing on their undertakings.

outliers.note: Records the rabbinic tradition that the man of God was Amos the father of Isaiah, and rejects it as without foundation.

themes: the LORD is not with Ephraim
a present God over a hired army

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil judge that a negative 'and not' has dropped from the text: the prophet's real sense is 'go alone and God will NOT let thee fall'; no version preserves the negative, so the loss is ancient.
Gill reads 'if thou wilt go, do it, be strong' as pure irony — go with Israel and mark the issue.
Wesley: 'do it' is an ironical concession, like 'go, and prosper.'

debates.question: How is 'God shall make thee fall before the enemy' to be read?

sides.position: an ironical concession in the received text — go with Israel and God will make thee fall
a negative has dropped out; the true sense is 'go alone and God will not let thee fall'

themes: God has power to help and to cast down

schools.summary: Keil records the LORD's promise of 'much more' and the dismissal of the hired band; Ellicott glosses the king's blunt 'what to do?' and identifies the troop of mercenaries.
Gill hears the king's reluctance, loath to lose so large a sum already advanced.
Henry makes it a lesson on obedience: God's all-sufficiency repays every loss — the hundred talents came back as tribute to Jotham in 2 Chronicles 27:5.

themes: the LORD able to give much more
God repays what is given up

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the separation of the Ephraimite host and their heat of anger — incensed at the apparent distrust and robbed of the plunder of victory.
Clarke: they thought themselves insulted and meditated revenge; Wesley reckons the double grievance of disgrace and lost spoil, the talents having gone to their officers only.
Gill: the king separated them from the army in which they had been ranked.
Henry sets the king's costly obedience — losing money, ally, and a fourth of his army rather than offend God — against the mercenaries' wounded pride.

themes: resentment that will turn to bloodshed

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil tie 'strengthened himself' to the prophet's 'be strong for the battle,' place the fight in the Valley of Salt SE of the Dead Sea (cf. 2 Samuel 8:13), and note the taking of Sela/Joktheel from 2 Kings 14:7.
Gill: undiscouraged by the dismissal, the king trusted the promise and power of God and went with boldness.
Henry counts the ten thousand left dead on the field of battle.

themes: strengthened himself per the prophet's word
faith vindicated with a smaller army
victory over the children of Seir

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the casting of the ten thousand from the head of Sela/Petra; Ellicott sets the massacre among ancient-warfare atrocities and defends its historicity against Thenius's text-corruption theory.
Gill records the equal number of Edomites taken captive.
Henry names the deed a severe cruelty, its provocation untold, staining a victory already won.

debates.question: Is the massacre of the prisoners a genuine tradition or a corruption of the Kings text?

sides.position: credible independent detail the chronicler preserves though Kings omits it
a garbled attempt to restore an illegible text of 2 Kings 14:7 about the capture of Sela

themes: ten thousand cast from the rock

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the plunder from Samaria to Beth-horon (cf. Job 1:17; 1 Chronicles 7:24) and dispute whether the raid was made on the homeward march or mounted afresh from Samaria, Ellicott suspecting 'Samaria' corrupt.
Wesley reads the raid as God's chastisement of the border cities' idolatry, caught from Israel and now punished by Israel's hand.
Gill identifies the raiders as the dismissed hundred thousand mercenaries.
Henry: God's way is in the sea — Satan both tempts and torments, corrupting Judah's border towns and then scourging them by the same men.

debates.question: Did the mercenaries raid on their way home, or return and set out afresh from Samaria?

sides.position: they plundered the cities on the homeward march
Samaria is the starting-point of a later, deliberate incursion (or the word is corrupt)

themes: obedience overruled to a further end

schools.summary: Keil fixes the setting up and worship of the Edomite gods; Ellicott illumines the custom of carrying off conquered idols from Assyrian inscriptions, holds the notice genuine additional information, and argues the idolatry need not mean abandoning Jehovah.
Henry marvels at the absurdity of worshipping the gods of a nation just conquered, gods that could not save their own — a folly perhaps visited on him for the cruelty to the prisoners.
Clarke gives the Targum's identification of the idols as the gods of the children of Gebal.

debates.question: Is Amaziah's idolatry genuine tradition, and how does it square with 2 Kings 14:3?

sides.position: genuine additional information from an independent source; it need not mean he forsook Jehovah
a contradiction of Kings, inferred by the chronicler from the king's later defeat

outliers.note: Holds that setting up the Edomite gods need not imply Amaziah abandoned the worship of Jehovah, a syncretism like that of Ahaz.

themes: the absurdity of bowing to defeated gods
the hinge from victory to ruin

schools.summary: Keil fixes the prophet's unanswerable question about gods that could not save their own; Ellicott sharpens 'delivered not,' compares Sennacherib (2 Kings 18:33), and names the likely Edomite deities Hadad, Kôsh, and Moloch from the inscriptions.
Gill: idolatry always provokes God, most of all when the king worships the very gods of the enemies God had given into his hand.
Henry: God sent to convince before he sent to destroy — consider the impotence of what men run to when they forsake God, and they would not so wrong themselves.

themes: gods that could not save their own

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the prophet turn the king's own word 'counsel' back on him — 'God hath counselled to destroy thee'; Keil reads the royal plural and the prophet's ceasing at the threat.
Henry: the king who gladly parted with his talents of silver would not part with his gods of silver, silencing and threatening the prophet — 'joined to idols, let him alone' (Hosea 4:17).
Wesley: the secure sinner prides himself on silencing his monitors, a plain sign he is marked for ruin; the deaf to reproof are ripening for destruction.
Gill: though no privy councillor, the prophet was appointed a counsellor by the King of kings, whom the king was bound to hear.

themes: God hath counselled to destroy thee
deaf to reproof, ripe for ruin

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott fix the challenge to Joash ('let us look one another in the face') and its parallel at 2 Kings 14:8, the counsel opposite to the prophet's of v.16.
Henry reads the challenge through Solomon's proverbs (Proverbs 29:23; 25:8): the king took the advice of flattering statesmen, not the prophet, and pride hurried him to his fall.
Gill: he took advice, not of God or his prophets, but of nobles as vain as himself.
Wesley: good to take advice, but of those fit to advise — he consulted his flatterers, not the prophet.

themes: one victory breeds a reckless war

schools.summary: Keil relates the fable of the thistle presuming on the cedar and trodden by a passing wild beast — a picture of the small king puffed up to challenge the greater.
Clarke points to the fuller parallel at 2 Kings 14:9 and gives the Targum's application binding the taunt to the dismissed mercenaries' raid of v.13.
Henry: Joash's answer was haughty and scornful, yet held friendly advice to sit still — a warning the proud king would not take from an enemy.

themes: the fable of the thistle and cedar
a last chance to draw back

schools.summary: Ellicott traces the fine textual differences from 2 Kings 14:10 (matters of pointing — hinneh/hakkeh, 'to get glory' used only here); Keil gives the plain sense: abide at home, why meddle with misfortune and fall, thou and Judah with thee.
Henry hears the friendly core of the scornful reply — the sound advice of Proverbs 25:8 to sit still, which the proud king could not take from an enemy.

Ellicott marks the clause as the chronicler's own, accounting for the king's infatuation by divine predetermination (cf. 2 Chronicles 25:16; 24:24; 10:15) — delivered into the hand of Joash because they had sought the gods of Edom; Keil reads it identically.
Gill: Amaziah would not hear the advice not to meddle to his own hurt.
Henry: his imprudence is made the punishment of his impiety — God left him to himself, and those who will not do well for their souls are given up to their own ruinous counsels.
Ellicott notes the clause stands as in 2 Kings 14:12 (omitted by Syriac and Arabic); Keil narrates the meeting at Beth-shemesh of Judah, the rout, and the flight of every man to his tent.
Henry names it the defeat that mortified the proud king — the fable fulfilled and the judgment of v.20 worked out.

Ellicott resolves the textual knots — 'Jehoahaz' for 'Ahaziah' (cf. 2 Kings 14:13), and 'the gate that turneth' for the 'corner gate' (cf. Ezekiel 8:3; 2 Chronicles 26:9), matters of pointing only; Keil fixes the capture and the four-hundred-cubit breach of Jerusalem's wall.
Henry reads the capture and the breached wall as the harvest of the king's proud challenge, the nation suffering for the pride of its throne.

themes: the conqueror of Edom made prisoner
the nation punished for royal pride

schools.summary: Clarke ties the seized treasure to the hereditary Levitical custody of Obed-edom's line over the house of Asuppim (1 Chronicles 26:15), and points to 2 Kings 14:14 for the hostages; Wesley glosses Obed-edom as the clan entrusted with the sacred treasures.
Ellicott notes the verb 'he took' has dropped from the Hebrew (an ancient omission), and judges 'with Obed-edom' the chronicler's own addition from an old document.
Ellicott fixes the verse as identical with 2 Kings 14:17, the synchronism of Amaziah's fifteen-year survival of the northern king Joash.
Clarke reads the fifteen years as embittered and unpopular, the defeated king lingering under the resentment of subjects humiliated by the lost war.
Henry: from his departure from the LORD his subjects' hearts departed from him, the war exasperating them more than the idolatry, and the conspiracy already forming.

themes: fifteen years' survival of his conqueror

schools.summary: Keil refers the acts to 'the book of the kings of Judah and Israel'; Ellicott renders 'the former and the latter,' notes the faulty Hebrew blending the chronicler's 'they are written' with the Kings formula 'are they not written,' and would follow the versions.
Clarke gives the Targum's moral reading of 'first and last' — the first when Amaziah walked in the fear of the LORD, the last when he departed from the right way.

themes: the book of the kings of Judah and Israel
first and last — a reign of two halves

schools.summary: Keil narrates the conspiracy, flight to Lachish, and death, and mends 'city of Judah' to 'city of David'; Ellicott binds the whole catastrophe to the king's apostasy, calling it the fulfilment of the prophet's word at v.16.
Clarke: unpopular after the defeat, Amaziah fled to Lachish but his murderers pursued — he who forsook the LORD was forsaken by every friend and perished in his gainsaying.
Henry: as he departed from the LORD his subjects' hearts departed from him; the conspirators were unrighteous, but God was righteous in it.

Keil and Ellicott record the burial with his fathers, refer 'upon horses' to 2 Kings 14:20, and agree that 'city of Judah' is a scribal error for 'city of David,' as the parallel, the versions, and some Hebrew manuscripts read.

themes: 'city of Judah' a slip for 'city of David'
a formal honour over a ruined reign
